subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun and Priya Share a Pizza
hook: Learn fractions by sharing pizza and sweets with Arjun and Priya!

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: A pizza-loving 12-year-old learning to share fairly

slides.title: A Pizza Divided
slides.storyContext: At a cafe, Arjun and Priya order a pizza cut into 8 equal slices. Arjun takes 3 slices. That's 3/8 of the pizza, says Priya. The top number tells us how many parts we have. The bottom number tells us how many equal parts the whole pizza is cut into.
slides.inSimpleWords: A fraction shows a part of a whole.

image.alt: A Pizza Divided — Working with Fractions

slides.title: Numerator and Denominator
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches: In 3/8, the 3 is the numerator - the number on top, showing how many parts we have. The 8 is the denominator - the number on bottom, showing the total parts. She draws a pizza diagram. If we have 3/8, we're missing 5/8. Together: 3/8 + 5/8 = 8/8 = 1 whole pizza!

points.label: Parts of a Fraction
points.text: Numerator (top): parts we have. Denominator (bottom): total parts the whole is divided into.

example.solution: 5 = parts we have. 12 = total parts in the whole

slides.inSimpleWords: Top number = parts we have. Bottom number = total parts.

image.alt: Numerator and Denominator — Working with Fractions

slides.title: Adding Fractions (Same Denominator)
slides.storyContext: Priya has 2/8 of a barfi. Arjun has 3/8. Let's combine them! says Priya. 2/8 + 3/8: we just add the top numbers and keep the bottom. 2 + 3 = 5, so we get 5/8.

points.label: Adding Fractions
points.text: If denominators are the same, add numerators: a/c + b/c = (a+b)/c

slides.inSimpleWords: Add fractions by adding tops if bottoms match.

image.alt: Adding Fractions (Same Denominator) — Working with Fractions

slides.title: Finding Common Denominators
slides.storyContext: Arjun has 1/2 of a gulab jamun. Priya has 1/3. Can we add these? asks Arjun. Priya thinks. 1/2 = 3/6 and 1/3 = 2/6. Now they have the same bottom! 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6! Arjun's eyes light up. We found a common denominator!

points.label: Common Denominators
points.text: Rewrite fractions so they have the same denominator. Find the LCM of the denominators.

slides.inSimpleWords: Make bottoms the same before adding fractions.

image.alt: Finding Common Denominators — Working with Fractions

slides.title: Multiplying Fractions
slides.storyContext: Arjun says: What's 1/2 of 2/3 of a chocolate bar? Priya multiplies: 1/2 x 2/3: multiply tops and bottoms. (1x2)/(2x3) = 2/6 = 1/3. She shades a bar to show. Yes, exactly 1/3 of a bar!
slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply fractions by multiplying tops and bottoms.

image.alt: Multiplying Fractions — Working with Fractions

slides.title: Equivalent Fractions
slides.storyContext: Priya draws two pizzas: one cut into 4 slices with 2 shaded, another cut into 8 slices with 4 shaded. Look! 2/4 and 4/8 show the same amount - they're equivalent fractions! Multiply or divide top and bottom by the same number.

points.label: Equivalent Fractions
points.text: 2/4 = 4/8 = 1/2. Multiply or divide top and bottom by the same number.

slides.inSimpleWords: Same amount can be written as different fractions.

image.alt: Equivalent Fractions — Working with Fractions

slides.title: Pizza Math Mastered
slides.storyContext: Walking home, Arjun and Priya review: Fractions have numerators and denominators. We add by finding common bottoms. We multiply by multiplying tops and bottoms. Equivalent fractions show the same parts differently. Arjun smiles. Now I can split anything fairly!

points.label: Fraction Mastery
points.text: Understand parts and wholes. Add with common denominators. Multiply numerators and denominators. Simplify to equivalent fractions.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions are parts of wholes, shared and calculated.

image.alt: Pizza Math Mastered — Working with Fractions

subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun and Priya Discover Number Magic
hook: Explore factors, multiples, and prime numbers in this fun number adventure!

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: A number theorist revealing number secrets

slides.title: What Divides Into 12?
slides.storyContext: At home, Arjun arranges 12 candies in rows. I can make 2 rows of 6, or 3 rows of 4, or 4 rows of 3! Priya nods. Those are factors of 12 - numbers that divide evenly into 12. Factors of 12 are: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12.
slides.inSimpleWords: Factors divide evenly into a number.

image.alt: What Divides Into 12? — Number Play

slides.title: Prime and Composite Numbers
slides.storyContext: Priya shows Arjun cards with numbers: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. Like 7 - only 1 and 7 divide into it! She shows another: 12 has many factors. It's composite. Arjun asks: Is 1 prime? Priya shakes her head. 1 is special - neither prime nor composite.

points.label: Prime vs. Composite
points.text: Prime: exactly 2 factors (1 and itself). Examples: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13. Composite: more than 2 factors. Example: 12.

slides.inSimpleWords: Prime numbers only divide by 1 and themselves.

image.alt: Prime and Composite Numbers — Number Play

slides.title: Multiples — Skip Counting
slides.storyContext: Priya counts: Multiples of 3 are: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18... She hops on a number line. Each time, I skip by 3. These are all multiples of 3 - they all have 3 as a factor!

points.label: Multiples
points.text: Multiples of n: n×1, n×2, n×3... Example: multiples of 5 are 5, 10, 15, 20...

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiples are what you get by skip-counting.

image.alt: Multiples — Skip Counting — Number Play

slides.title: GCD — Finding the Greatest Common Factor
slides.storyContext: Arjun has 12 marbles, Priya has 18. They want to divide them into equal piles with no leftovers. What's the largest pile size that works for both? asks Arjun. Priya lists: Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. The greatest common factor is 6! They make 2 piles of 6 marbles each.

points.label: GCD (Greatest Common Divisor)
points.text: The largest number that divides evenly into two numbers. GCD(12, 18) = 6

slides.inSimpleWords: GCD is the largest number dividing both.

image.alt: GCD — Finding the Greatest Common Factor — Number Play

slides.title: LCM — Finding the Least Common Multiple
slides.storyContext: Arjun's bus comes every 4 minutes. Priya's comes every 6 minutes. When will both buses arrive together? Priya calculates: Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20... Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24... The least common multiple is 12. Both buses arrive together every 12 minutes!

points.label: LCM (Least Common Multiple)
points.text: The smallest number that is a multiple of both. LCM(4, 6) = 12

slides.inSimpleWords: LCM is the smallest number both divide into.

image.alt: LCM — Finding the Least Common Multiple — Number Play

slides.title: Divisibility Rules Make It Faster
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches shortcuts: A number is divisible by 2 if it's even. By 3 if its digit sum is divisible by 3. By 5 if it ends in 0 or 5. By 10 if it ends in 0. She checks 135: 1+3+5=9, which is divisible by 3, so 135 is too! Arjun tries 156: 1+5+6=12, divisible by 3! 156 ÷ 3 = 52!

points.label: Divisibility Shortcuts
points.text: Divisible by 2: even. By 3: digit sum is divisible by 3. By 5: ends in 0/5. By 10: ends in 0.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use shortcuts to check if numbers divide evenly.

image.alt: Divisibility Rules Make It Faster — Number Play

slides.title: The World of Number Patterns
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya review their number adventure: factors, primes, composites, multiples, GCD, LCM. Numbers have hidden patterns! says Arjun. Priya smiles. Yes. And now you can see them all.

points.label: Number Fundamentals
points.text: Factors divide into numbers. Primes have 2 factors. Multiples are skip-counted. GCD and LCM solve shared problems.

slides.inSimpleWords: Number patterns connect factors, multiples, and primes.

image.alt: The World of Number Patterns — Number Play

subject: Science
title: Arjun and Priya's Garden Adventure
hook: Discover how plants make their own food in this green story!

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: A curious gardener wondering how plants grow

slides.title: Why Do Plants Need Roots?
slides.storyContext: In their school garden, Arjun plants a seed. Priya says: The roots do two important jobs. First, they hold the plant in soil so it doesn't tip over. Second, they absorb water and minerals from the soil - that's nutrition! Arjun digs carefully. So roots are like a food pipeline?
slides.inSimpleWords: Roots absorb water and minerals for plant nutrition.

image.alt: Why Do Plants Need Roots? — Nutrition in Plants

slides.title: Green Power — Photosynthesis
slides.storyContext: Priya points at the green leaves. Inside these leaves, plants have a special power! They trap sunlight and use it to make food from water and air. It's called photosynthesis! She writes: Sunlight + Water + Carbon Dioxide = Glucose (sugar) + Oxygen.

points.label: Photosynthesis
points.text: Plants make glucose (food) using sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide. They release oxygen as a bonus!

example.problem: What three things does a plant need for photosynthesis?
example.solution: Sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide (from air)

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants make food using sun, water, and air.

image.alt: Green Power — Photosynthesis — Nutrition in Plants

slides.title: Chlorophyll — The Green Pigment
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: Why are leaves green? Priya smiles. Because of chlorophyll - a green pigment inside leaf cells. It captures sunlight! She holds up a leaf to the sun. Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light, but reflects green light. That's why it looks green to us!

points.label: Chlorophyll
points.text: Green pigment in plant cells that captures sunlight for photosynthesis. It absorbs red/blue light and reflects green.

slides.inSimpleWords: Chlorophyll is the green pigment that traps sunlight.

image.alt: Chlorophyll — The Green Pigment — Nutrition in Plants

slides.title: Heterotrophic Plants — Dodder and Mistletoe
slides.storyContext: Priya points at a vine wrapping around a tree. Not all plants are green! Some, like dodder, can't make their own food. They're parasites - they steal nutrients from other plants! Arjun shivers. That's mean! Priya nods. It's nature's strategy. Most plants are autotrophs and make their own food. A few are parasites.

points.label: Autotrophs vs. Parasites
points.text: Autotrophs (like most plants) make their own food. Parasites (like dodder) steal food from host plants.

slides.inSimpleWords: Most plants make food. Some steal it from other plants.

image.alt: Heterotrophic Plants — Dodder and Mistletoe — Nutrition in Plants

slides.title: Minerals Plants Need
slides.storyContext: Priya shows a withered plant next to a healthy one. This plant had water but lacked nutrients. Plants need: nitrogen (for growth), phosphorus (for roots and flowers), potassium (for strength). She sprinkles fertilizer on the soil. Now it has all the minerals it needs!

points.label: Essential Minerals
points.text: Nitrogen: growth. Phosphorus: roots/flowers. Potassium: strength. Plants absorb these through roots.

example.problem: Why do farmers add fertilizer to soil?
example.solution: To provide nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium plants need for healthy growth

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants need minerals from soil for good health.

image.alt: Minerals Plants Need — Nutrition in Plants

slides.title: Transpiration — Plants Release Water
slides.storyContext: Arjun covers a plant with a plastic bag. Within hours, water droplets appear inside. Where did that come from? he asks. Priya explains: Plants absorb more water than they use. They release extra water vapor through leaves - that's transpiration. The bag traps it, showing us!

points.label: Transpiration
points.text: Plants release water vapor through leaves. It's like plant sweating on a hot day.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants release water through leaves as vapor.

image.alt: Transpiration — Plants Release Water — Nutrition in Plants

slides.title: The Complete Plant Story
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya sit under a mango tree. Roots absorb water and minerals. Leaves capture sunlight and make food. Plants release oxygen for us to breathe and water for the ecosystem. Everything is connected! says Priya. Arjun smiles. Plants are farmers of sunlight!

points.label: Plant Nutrition Summary
points.text: Roots absorb water/minerals. Photosynthesis makes food. Chlorophyll captures light. Plants are autotrophs except parasites.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants are self-feeding organisms using sun energy.

image.alt: The Complete Plant Story — Nutrition in Plants
